title: Source generators and compile-time code
body: A source generator is a compiler plug-in that inspects your code during compilation and adds new C# source files to it. Generated code is ordinary code: it is type-checked, debuggable and AOT-friendly, which makes generators the modern replacement for many uses of reflection.

The BCL ships several. `[GeneratedRegex("pattern")]` on a `partial` method or (since C# 13) a partial property produces an optimized regular-expression implementation at build time. `System.Text.Json` source generation (`JsonSerializerContext`) produces serializers without reflection. `[LibraryImport]` generates P/Invoke marshalling, and logging's `[LoggerMessage]` generates allocation-free log methods.

The pattern is always the same: you write a `partial` declaration plus an attribute, and the generator writes the other half. That is why partial methods, properties, constructors and events keep expanding in recent C# versions. Writing your own generator means an `IIncrementalGenerator` in a separate analyzer project targeting .NET Standard 2.0, referenced with `OutputItemType="Analyzer"`.

Generated files can be inspected: set `EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles` to true in the project, or open the Analyzers node in an IDE. Generators must be incremental and deterministic so builds stay fast and reproducible.
Prefer a built-in generator when one exists (regex, JSON, logging, interop). Check that the generated code is what you expect and that the generator is pinned to a version, like any other dependency.
challenge: Use [GeneratedRegex] to write a partial method Hex() matching a # followed by exactly six hex digits (ignore case), and print which of #A1B2C3, #12345, abc123 match.
question: What does a source generator add to a compilation?
correct: New C# source code that is compiled with your project
wrong: IL patched into the binary after compilation
reasoning: Generators emit ordinary source during the build, so the result is type-checked and works with trimming and AOT.
